newsitem.title: UK: UK's Rifkind says single currency unlikely in 1999.
newsitem.headline: UK's Rifkind says single currency unlikely in 1999.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Sunday it was unlikely a single European currency would be formed in 1999.
"A single currency is unlikely to actually happen in any country in 1999," Rifkind said on Independent Television, basing his prognosis on analysis by finance minister Kenneth Clarke.

"If it did happen, it would be essentially for political reasons, that the the convergence criteria were not being properly respected and on that basis it would be very unlikely that the United Kingdom would wish to join."

He said there were clear reasons why German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, European Commission President Jacques Santer and French President Jacques Chirac would not acknowledge any possibility of delay in the single currency being launched on target in 1999.

"There are strong political reasons why they have to maintain that position. They may believe it, I'm not questioning their sincerity but they also do have a domestic political imperative," Rifkind said.
He said there have recently been moves that "could best be described as creative accountancy" in some European countries.
These are moves "which don't actually point to genuine sustainable convergence but which help produce the kind of figures that may be necessary to meet the convergence criteria."
But it was too early to say whether the moves taken so far would discredit the whole exercise.
"About a year from now the countries of the European Union will have to meet and by a majority vote decide which countries join a single currency," he said.
"In the case of the United Kingdom we are not by any means convinced that we even want to join the single currency."
